description: Baseline permissions for the main window. The permission list holds exactly two entries, `core:event:allow-listen` and `core:event:allow-unlisten`, added together at Phase 2d-5-7a when `src/lib/components/AppShell.svelte` first registered the frontend's one event listener (`workspace://reconciliation-ready`, through `src/lib/ipc/events.ts`). Tauri's `listen` is a PLUGIN command — it invokes `plugin:event|listen` — and a plugin command is access-checked even from the application's own origin, so the first entry is what lets the registration succeed at all; the unlisten function that registration resolves with invokes a second plugin command, `plugin:event|unlisten`, gated by the second entry, and granting the first alone would leave a Rust-side listener that disposal cannot remove. Neither `core:event:default` nor any wildcard is used: the default set also grants `allow-emit` and `allow-emit-to`, which would let a compromised renderer emit events into the application's own event system, and nothing in this frontend emits. The list was EMPTY from Phase 1b-1's review through Phase 2d-5-6, including for the localized macOS menu that Phase 1b-1 expected would need the first entry. The previous value before that, `core:default`, was not minimal — it expands to the path, event, window, webview, image, menu and tray defaults, and the image defaults alone (`image:allow-from-path`, `image:allow-rgba`) would let a compromised renderer load a local image path and read its pixels. Nothing here grants the menu anything: the frontend does not build menus — it hands the translated labels to this application's own `set_menu_labels` command, which Rust builds the menu from. `core:menu`'s permissions (`menu:allow-new`, `menu:allow-set-as-app-menu`, and the rest) are what a renderer that drove `@tauri-apps/api/menu` itself would need, and granting them would let a compromised renderer replace the application menu with items of its own choosing. This is not an argument: `src-tauri/src/dispatch_check.rs` drives all seventeen application commands through the real dispatcher with this file and the shipped `tauri.conf.json`, drives `plugin:event|listen` and `plugin:event|unlisten` from the local origin, asserts through the resolved access-control list that `plugin:event|emit` and `plugin:event|emit_to` stay refused, and `a_remote_origin_is_refused` attempts all seventeen application commands and both event-plugin commands from a remote origin — its application-command table is compared with the names parsed out of `generate_handler!`, so a command added and not swept fails that test. This application publishes no ACL manifest for its own commands, so there is no permission a capability could name to let a remote origin reach one; adding a `remote` block to this file was measured and changes nothing, and this file has none. Every later phase enumerates the narrowest permissions its feature needs — never a wildcard, and never a `*:default` set.
